live_plab_copy.takeaway: Painless indurated genital ulcer: primary syphilis; painful ulcers: herpes.

A patient with recurrent genital herpes asks why the lesions keep returning.

Which explanation is correct?

options.A: The virus remains only on the skin surface
options.B: Recurrences are caused by a new bacterial infection
options.C: Herpes simplex virus remains latent in sensory nerve ganglia
options.D: The infection is completely eradicated after the first episode
options.E: Recurrences occur only after reinfection from another person

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Herpes simplex virus remains latent in sensory nerve ganglia
live_plab_copy.why_correct: HSV establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglia and can reactivate periodically.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. HSV becomes latent in sensory ganglia, not on the skin surface. B. Recurrences are caused by viral reactivation, not bacterial infection. D. HSV is not eradicated after the first episode. E. Recurrences usually reflect reactivation of latent virus, not reinfection.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Herpes simplex virus travels along sensory nerves and stays latent in the ganglia for life; reactivation causes recurrences, which are usually milder and shorter than the first episode.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Recurrent genital herpes ↓ After the first infection HSV travels up sensory nerves ↓ It lies latent in the ganglia and reactivates ↓ HSV remains latent in sensory nerve ganglia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, recurrences occur only after reinfection — tempting because herpes is sexually transmitted, but recurrences come from the patient's own latent virus, not new exposure.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Herpes recurrences are reactivation from latent virus in sensory ganglia.

What is the key principle?

options.A: Perform lumbar puncture first, then give antibiotics once CSF is obtained

live_plab_copy.pearl: In suspected bacterial meningitis, never delay antibiotics for CT or lumbar puncture; signs of raised intracranial pressure make lumbar puncture unsafe until it is reassessed.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Suspected meningitis ↓ Features of raised intracranial pressure ↓ LP may cause harm, but delaying antibiotics is dangerous ↓ Assess LP safety; do not delay antibiotics
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, CT head and withholding antibiotics until reported — tempting as imaging seems a sensible safety step, but delaying antibiotics worsens outcomes in meningitis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected meningitis: antibiotics first; lumbar puncture only when safe.

A patient has suspected C. difficile infection in hospital.

Which principle is appropriate?

options.A: Nurse in an open bay and clean hands with alcohol gel after contact
options.B: Isolate with enteric precautions and review unnecessary antibiotics
options.C: Start loperamide to reduce diarrhoea and environmental spread
options.D: Continue current antibiotics to avoid interrupting treatment
options.E: Wait for the stool test result before starting any precautions

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Isolate with enteric precautions and review unnecessary antibiotics
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Suspected C. difficile infection needs prompt isolation with enteric precautions, hand washing with soap and water, and review and stopping of unnecessary antibiotics, in line with NICE NG199 and UKHSA guidance.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores, and an open bay risks spread; isolation and soap-and-water hand washing are needed. C. Antimotility drugs such as loperamide should be avoided in suspected C. difficile infection. D. Continuing unnecessary antibiotics perpetuates C. difficile infection; they should be reviewed and stopped where possible. E. Precautions should start on clinical suspicion, not after results.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In suspected C. difficile infection, isolate with enteric precautions, wash hands with soap and water because alcohol gel does not kill spores, and stop unnecessary antibiotics.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Hospital patient ↓ Suspected C. difficile infection ↓ Spores spread easily and resist alcohol gel ↓ Isolate with enteric precautions and review antibiotics
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, waiting for the stool result — testing feels evidence-based, but precautions must start on clinical suspicion to prevent spread on the ward.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected C. difficile: isolate now, use soap and water, and stop unnecessary antibiotics.

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Hepatitis C is primarily blood-borne, and sharing injecting equipment is a major transmission route.

live_plab_copy.stem: A person has evidence of previous exposure to tuberculosis but has no symptoms and no evidence of active disease. What is this state called?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Latent TB infection describes infection with M. tuberculosis without clinical evidence of active disease.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Miliary TB is disseminated active TB. C. Active pulmonary TB causes clinical disease. D. Tuberculous meningitis is active infection involving the central nervous system. E. Multidrug resistance describes antimicrobial resistance, not simply asymptomatic infection.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Latent TB is asymptomatic and not infectious; it is detected by a tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, and treatment reduces the risk of later reactivation.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Evidence of previous TB exposure ↓ No symptoms ↓ No active disease ↓ Infected but contained ↓ Latent tuberculosis infection
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, Active pulmonary tuberculosis — evidence of exposure tempts, but active disease needs clinical or radiological features, which are absent here.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Infected, asymptomatic and not infectious: latent TB.

live_plab_copy.stem: How is pulmonary tuberculosis most commonly transmitted?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Pulmonary TB is transmitted through inhalation of airborne particles containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. TB is not transmitted by mosquitoes. B. Contaminated water is not the usual route of pulmonary TB transmission. D. Food is not the usual route of pulmonary TB transmission. E. Faecal–oral transmission is associated with infections such as hepatitis A.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, Contaminated food — unpasteurised milk can transmit bovine TB, but pulmonary TB in people spreads by inhalation, not food.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Pulmonary TB spreads through the air: isolate infectious patients and trace contacts.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Meningococcus spreads by respiratory droplets and close contact; contacts need prophylaxis.

A blood culture grows an organism that is a common skin contaminant, while the patient is clinically well and repeat cultures are negative.

What should be considered?

options.D: Early septic shock requiring fluid resuscitation

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Growth of a common skin organism (such as coagulase-negative staphylococci) in a single culture from a clinically well patient with negative repeat cultures most likely represents contamination. Results must be interpreted with the clinical picture.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Endocarditis typically produces persistently positive cultures, not a single positive with negative repeats. B. A likely skin contaminant in a well patient with negative repeats does not justify broad-spectrum antibiotics. D. Septic shock is unlikely in a clinically well patient. E. Meningitis is diagnosed by clinical features and CSF analysis, not a single possibly contaminated blood culture.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A single culture growing a skin organism such as coagulase-negative staphylococci in a clinically well patient with negative repeats most likely reflects contamination.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Microbiology results must be interpreted alongside the clinical picture and other cultures.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, occult bacteraemia needing broad-spectrum cover — a positive culture tempts treatment, but a likely contaminant in a well patient with negative repeats does not justify it.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Interpret a positive blood culture with the patient, not in isolation.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient remains positive for hepatitis B surface antigen for more than 6 months.

What does this indicate?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Persistence of HBsAg for more than 6 months is consistent with chronic hepatitis B infection.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Hepatitis A is a separate virus. B. Vaccination produces protective antibodies rather than persistent HBsAg. C. Hepatitis C antibodies do not indicate hepatitis B status. D. Resolved infection is associated with loss of HBsAg and development of appropriate antibodies.
live_plab_copy.pearl: HBsAg means current infection, and persistence beyond 6 months defines chronic hepatitis B; anti-HBs alone indicates vaccination, while anti-HBc with anti-HBs indicates past infection.
live_plab_copy.thinking: HBsAg positive ↓ Surface antigen = virus present ↓ Persists beyond 6 months ↓ Chronic hepatitis B infection
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, hepatitis B vaccination response — tempts as surface-related, but vaccination produces anti-HBs antibody, not HBsAg.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: HBsAg persisting beyond 6 months means chronic hepatitis B.
